lead: Stephen’s death does not silence the word; it scatters it. The reading from Acts begins in the same verse where Tuesday’s ended: a persecution, in which Saul took a leading part, drives the believers out of Jerusalem, and Philip brings the Gospel to Samaria, where “there was great joy in that city”. In the Gospel the discourse at Capernaum continues: the will of the Father is that nothing given to the Son should be lost. Psalm 66 calls all the earth to cry out to God with joy.

r.h: Those who were scattered proclaimed the word
set: Devout men bury Stephen with loud lamentation, and a severe persecution falls on the church in Jerusalem. Many scholars think it struck above all the Greek-speaking believers of Stephen’s circle, since the apostles were able to stay in the city. Philip, named next after Stephen in the list of the Seven (6:5), is not the apostle Philip.

Acts follows the plan announced by the risen Lord: “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8). With this reading the Gospel reaches Samaria. Jews and Samaritans had long been divided over worship and the Temple (John 4:9, 20), and the Samaritans too awaited one who was to come (John 4:25).
str: vv. 1b–3: persecution; Stephen’s burial; Saul ravages the church.
v. 4: the scattered believers proclaim the word.
vv. 5–8: Philip in Samaria: preaching, signs, healing and joy.
kw: The verb is built on speirō, “to sow”, the root of our word “diaspora”. What was meant to destroy the community sows it across the land.
A strong word, used of wild animals mauling or of an army laying waste. Paul himself later admits that he was violently persecuting the church of God (Galatians 1:13).
A mark of Luke’s writing, from the angels at Bethlehem (Luke 2:10) to the end of Acts. Here the joy belongs to a whole city of Samaritans.
vv: Now those who were scattered went from place to place, proclaiming the word.
Not the apostles but ordinary believers, refugees, are the first missionaries beyond Jerusalem.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.

Some ancient manuscripts read “the city”, others “a city”, and translations differ. If “the city” is meant, it may be the old capital, rebuilt by Herod the Great as Sebaste. Philip proclaims “the Messiah”: the Christ Samaria too was waiting for.
So there was great joy in that city.
The last words of the reading. Healing of body and spirit, together with the good news, bring joy.
ch: Tertullian wrote at the end of the second century that the blood of Christians is seed (in substance). Acts already shows the pattern: suffering does not end the mission; it carries it further. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the pilgrim Church is missionary by its very nature (Ad Gentes 2). Philip, counted by tradition among the first deacons and later called “the evangelist” (21:8), shows that the work of proclaiming belongs to more than the apostles. The Catechism adds that the Church on mission walks the road Christ walked, the way of poverty and obedience, of service and self-sacrifice even to death (CCC 852).

r.h: I will never drive away anyone who comes to me
set: The discourse at Capernaum continues. Verse 35 repeats the last line of Tuesday’s Gospel, “I am the bread of life”, and Jesus now speaks of the will of his Father. The crowd has seen him and yet does not believe (v. 36). Jesus answers, not with a new sign, but with a promise about all who come to him.
str: vv. 37–38: all that the Father gives will come; I will never drive them away; I came to do the will of the one who sent me.
vv. 39–40: the Father’s will: lose nothing, eternal life, “I will raise them up on the last day”.
kw: The word comes four times in vv. 38–40. Jesus said that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him (4:34); here we learn what that will is: that none be lost.
A strong double negative in Greek. In chapter 9 the man born blind will be driven out (9:34); whoever comes to Jesus is never driven out.
“I will raise them up on the last day” comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54). The bread of life leads to the resurrection of the body.
vv: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away;
God’s gift and our coming are held together. No one who comes is turned back, however late or however wounded.
for I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.
The Catechism quotes this verse in speaking of the whole life of Jesus as an offering to the Father, which leads him to the cross (CCC 606).
This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.”
Eternal life begins now, in believing; it is completed in the resurrection.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: it is he who on the last day will raise up those who have believed in him and who have eaten his body and drunk his blood (CCC 994). John 6:37–40 is one of the Gospels the Church offers for funeral Masses: at the grave the Church leans on the promise that the Son loses nothing the Father has given him.

study: When has a loss or a hardship in my life become, like the scattering in Acts, an opening for the Gospel?
Jesus says he will never drive away anyone who comes to him. Is there someone I keep at a distance whom he would welcome?
